newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator seeks interim nuke waste site by 2003.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator seeks interim nuke waste site by 2003.

text.p: Sen. Frank Murkowski Wednesday sought to win over opponents to building a temporary storage facility in Nevada for radioactive waste from nuclear plants by introducing a new bill with major changes.
However, a key sticking point remained, said Sen. Jeff Bingaman, a New Mexico Democrat who was involved in changing the legislation by the Alaska Republican.

Nuclear utilities are pressing for a temporary storage site until the government has a permanent dump ready to bury their waste. Under law, the Energy Department is supposed to start taking responsibility for the waste by February 1998.

But the government has nowhere to put it yet and does not expect to have a permanent dump ready until 2010 at the earliest. The only site being investigated as a permanent dump is Yucca Mountain in Nevada.

While Murkowski agreed to defer the opening of the storage facility to 2003 and to shrink its proposed size, he refused to drop a provision that would make the government put it in Nevada even if the mountain was found to be unsafe for a dump.
Bingaman said he would offer an amendment to eliminate the default provision.
"The question of what happens if Yucca Mountain is deemed unsafe remains a central issue," Bingaman said in a statement.
"It makes no sense to make Nevada the de facto waste storage site if Yucca Mountain is determined to be unsafe," he said in a statement. "It's not fair to Nevada, and it's not sound policy."

The White House has repeatedly said it would veto the original bill, because it did not want to start shipping the spent fuel from 80 plants across the country before it knew whether it could safely put a permanent dump in the mountain.

Murkowski's bill seeks to put a temporary storage facility at the Nevada Test Site next to Yucca Mountain, if the Energy Department determines next year that the mountain will be safe for burying nuclear waste.

If the government found the mountain to be unfit, then the president would have to choose another location to store the nuclear waste. If he failed to identify another site, the bill would clear the way for nuclear waste to be shipped to Nevada.
The Clinton administration has not commented on whether it could live with any of the changes proposed by Murkowski.
The Senate last year passed a bill similar to Murkowski's original proposal by a vote of 63-37, four votes short of a veto-proof majority.

Murkowksi said he was open to more changes in his bill to win more votes. "We will continue our quest for a compromise which can be supported by a bipartisan majority of the Congress and hopefully the president as well," he said on the Senate floor.
